VPC CIDR: 10.0.0.0/16 This address range contains 65,536 IPv4 addresses, from 10.0.0.0 through 10.0.255.255. You will divide part of this range into smaller subnet CIDR blocks. AWS reserves five addresses within each subnet.

You have already seen state in earlier chapters. When you run terraform plan, Terraform uses state to identify the resources it already manages and compares the configuration, state and refreshed infrastructure information to determine what should change. When you run terraform apply, Terraform updates the state to reflect the new or changed resources.
Terraform needs to know that this resource address (aws_vpc.main) corresponds to a specific VPC ID (vpc-12345678). State stores this mapping.
By default, Terraform stores state in a local file named terraform.tfstate in the working directory.
Some teams attempt to solve the collaboration problem by committing terraform.tfstate to Git. This is a bad practice for several reasons.

The AWS identity running Terraform needs permission to list the state bucket and read and write the state object. When use_lockfile = true, it also needs permission to create, read, and delete the associated .tflock object.
Without locking, two engineers could run terraform apply at the same time, causing:

When use_lockfile = true in the backend configuration, Terraform uses an S3 lock file associated with the state object. While one Terraform operation holds the lock, another operation cannot acquire it and safely modify the same state.

Older Terraform repositories may use dynamodb_table for state locking. DynamoDB-based S3 locking is deprecated; new configurations should use use_lockfile = true. You may still encounter the DynamoDB pattern in existing repositories.

State files may contain sensitive data. Amazon S3 automatically encrypts new objects at rest with SSE-S3 as the base encryption level. The backend's encrypt = true makes the encryption requirement explicit. Organisations that require control over encryption keys can instead use AWS KMS. A customer-managed KMS key also requires the Terraform identity to have the necessary KMS permissions.

The infrastructure from Chapters 4–7 is already managed in the default workspace. Do not create a new workspace and immediately apply the existing configuration, because the new workspace starts with an empty state and Terraform may propose creating another copy of the infrastructure.

A Terraform workspace allows you to manage multiple state instances using the same configuration. For example, you can create dev and staging workspaces, each tracking its own set of infrastructure resources. Switching workspaces changes the state Terraform uses when planning and applying changes, without changing the configuration itself. However, workspaces do not automatically change AWS accounts, Regions, credentials, or configuration values. They provide state separation, not account or security isolation.
dev workspace → separate state
prod workspace → separate state

Every Terraform working directory starts with a default workspace, and it cannot be deleted. If configuration maps values by terraform.workspace, make sure every workspace that might be active has a valid value—or avoid applying from default.

Refactoring with moved and removed Blocks

Terraform tracks every managed resource by its address — the combination of resource type and local name (for example, aws_vpc.main), plus any module path (for example, module.network.aws_vpc.main). State maps that address to a real AWS resource ID.
moved and removed blocks let you declare how Terraform should handle these state transitions as part of the configuration, so it can update state instead of destroying and recreating infrastructure.
moved Blocks

When you rename a resource or move it into a module, its Terraform address changes. Without a moved block, Terraform sees the old address disappear from configuration and a new address appear, and proposes to destroy the old resource and create a new one.
A moved block records the old address and the new address so Terraform can rewrite the address in state rather than treating the change as destruction and recreation:
Without a moved block, Terraform would interpret the address change as deleting the old resource and creating a new one.
With a moved block, Terraform updates the address in state:
To stop managing a resource without destroying it, use a removed block.
Replace the original resource block with the removed block. Also remove any remaining references to that resource from the configuration.
terraform validate helps identify references that still depend on the resource before you remove it from Terraform's management.
HashiCorp recommends removed blocks over terraform state rm because they can be reviewed through the normal plan/apply workflow.

terraform state mv and terraform state rm are advanced, imperative alternatives for one-off state operations. For normal configuration refactoring, prefer moved and removed blocks because the migration remains documented in code and visible during planning.
